historical_prediction: We included 11 studies with 414 participants that looked at using therapeutic ultrasound to treat carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The studies compared different ultrasound regimens, ultrasound with other non-surgical interventions, and ultrasound as part of a multi-component intervention with another non-surgical intervention. Most studies had an unclear or high risk of bias. There is limited evidence that therapeutic ultrasound may increase the chance of short-term overall improvement when compared to placebo or other non-surgical interventions, but this should be interpreted with caution due to study limitations. There is insufficient evidence to support one ultrasound regimen over another or to show that ultrasound is more effective than other non-surgical interventions for CTS. More high-quality studies are needed to determine the effectiveness and safety of therapeutic ultrasound for CTS. No studies reported any adverse effects, but this outcome was only measured in three studies.

This review looked at four studies that involved 2250 people who took either insulin detemir or glargine for 24 to 52 weeks. The studies had a high risk of bias. Insulin glargine was taken once daily in the evening, while insulin detemir was started once daily in the evening with an optional additional dose in the morning in three studies and twice daily in one study. By the end of the trial, 13.6% to 57.2% of people taking insulin detemir were injecting it twice daily.

Blood sugar control, measured by glycosylated haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and HbA1c of 7% or less with or without hypoglycaemia, did not differ significantly between the two treatment groups. There were no significant differences in overall, nocturnal, or severe hypoglycaemia between the two groups. Insulin detemir was associated with less weight gain, while insulin glargine resulted in a lower daily basal insulin dose and fewer injection site reactions.

There was no significant difference in the variability of fasting plasma glucose (FPG) or glucose values in 24-hour profiles between the two groups. The review did not find any significant differences in quality of life, costs, or mortality. Only one trial reported results on health-related quality of life, and there were no significant differences between treatment groups.

In summary, our analysis suggests that there is no clinically relevant difference in efficacy or safety between insulin detemir and insulin glargine for controlling high blood sugar. However, to achieve the same glycaemic control, insulin detemir was often injected twice daily in a higher dose but with less weight gain, while insulin glargine was injected once daily, with fewer injection site reactions.

We reviewed a single study of 125 patients who had surgery for a type of brain tumor called glioblastoma. The study compared having a brain scan within 48 hours after surgery to not having one. Most patients also received radiation therapy and temozolomide treatment.

The study found that having an early scan made little or no difference in the number of deaths at one year (48% vs 55%) or two years (86% vs 81) after diagnosis. There was very low certainty evidence for these findings. The study had some bias and only looked at this one imaging schedule.

There is little information on other imaging schedules or their impact on health outcomes. Current imaging schedules are mostly based on practical considerations rather than strong evidence.

Further research is needed to determine the optimal timing of surveillance imaging for different types of glioma, potentially through mathematical modelling and studies in pediatric glioma.

Three studies tested different treatments given before standard radiation therapy (RT) in 931 participants with anaplastic oligodendroglioma or anaplastic oligoastrocytoma brain tumors. None of the studies blinded participants or personnel, so they are at high risk of bias. The studies found that adding procarbazine, lomustine and vincristine (PCV) chemotherapy to RT improved overall survival (OS) compared to RT alone. This benefit was not seen in earlier analyses. Two studies also found that certain genetic markers, such as codeletion of chromosomes 1p and 19q with or without IDH-1 or -2 mutation, were associated with increased sensitivity to PCV and RT. However, PCV had significant side effects. It is unclear if temozolomide can be used instead. The role of biomarkers in identifying people who may benefit from PCV should be further studied.

Three studies with a total of 285 preterm babies (140 received arginine) were included. The quality of these studies was good. Preterm babies who received arginine had a lower risk of developing necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) compared to those who did not receive arginine (moderate quality evidence). The number needed to treat to prevent one case of NEC was 6 (95% CI 4 to 10). Arginine supplementation also reduced the risk of developing severe NEC (stage 3) and death related to NEC. No significant side effects directly attributable to arginine were reported. However, there was clinical heterogeneity in mortality rates. There is insufficient data at present to support a practice recommendation for administering arginine to preterm infants due to the small overall sample size. A larger multi-center randomized controlled study is needed.

We looked at 18 trials with 4843 participants who received bisphosphonates or a placebo to prevent bone problems caused by cancer that had spread to the bones.

The main result was that there was no clear difference in pain relief between those taking bisphosphonates and those not taking them (3 more people per 1000 had pain relief with bisphosphonates, but this could also mean 11 fewer or 14 more).

However, bisphosphonates probably reduced the number of bone-related problems in people with prostate cancer that had spread to the bones (58 fewer problems per 1000 people, 85 fewer to 27 fewer). There was no clear difference in death rates between those taking bisphosphonates and those not taking them.

Bisphosphonates probably increased the number of people who experienced nausea (7 more cases per 1000, 0 fewer to 14 more) and renal adverse events (22 more cases per 1000, 4 more to 50 more). There was no clear difference in the number of participants with osteonecrosis of the jaw between groups.

Bisphosphonates probably decreased the number of participants with disease progression. However, these benefits need to be weighed against the increased risk of renal impairment and nausea in men receiving bisphosphonates. Future studies should focus on patient-important outcomes such as quality of life and pain using standardized assessment tools.

We looked at two studies from 1987 and 2004 with a total of 148 people who had heart valve surgery. Both studies had a high risk of bias. There wasn't enough evidence at the 3 to 6 months follow-up to determine the effect of exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation compared to no exercise on death (RR 4.46 (95% CI 0.22 to 90.78)) or serious side effects (RR 1.15 (95% CI 0.37 to 3.62)). The studies did not report on health-related quality of life, return to work, New York Heart Association class, left ventricular ejection fraction, or cost. However, the studies found that exercise-based rehabilitation may increase exercise capacity (SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.81 to -0.13). There was insufficient evidence at 12 months follow-up for the return to work outcome (RR 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.56)). Due to limited information, trial sequential analysis could not be performed as planned. Our findings suggest that exercise-based rehabilitation for adults after heart valve surgery may improve exercise capacity. However, due to a lack of evidence, we cannot evaluate the impact on other outcomes such as mortality and quality of life. More high-quality randomised clinical trials are needed to assess the impact of exercise-based rehabilitation on patient-relevant outcomes.

Two studies were included in this review. The first study looked at two procedures for treating urethral stricture disease in 210 adult men. There was no significant difference in the number of men who were free from strictures after three years or in the time it took for the strictures to come back. The second study compared two different treatments for traumatic stricture of the posterior urethra following pelvic fracture injury in 50 men. In the first six months, more men in the urethrotomy group needed additional surgery compared to those in the primary urethroplasty group. After two years, a larger number of men in the urethrotomy group required continued self-dilatation or further surgery for stricture recurrence compared to those treated with primary urethroplasty. There is not enough information to determine which treatment is best for urethral stricture disease in terms of balancing efficacy, adverse effects and costs. More research is needed to answer relevant clinical questions regarding the treatment of men with urethral strictures.

A study including 39 people with sickle cell disease was analyzed. Participants were given oral vitamin D or a placebo for six weeks and followed up to six months. The study found that:

- At eight, 16, and 24 weeks, the vitamin D group had significantly higher levels of vitamin D in their blood compared to the placebo group.
- There was no significant difference in side effects (tingling of lips or hands) between the two groups.
- The vitamin D group reported fewer pain days than the placebo group at 24 weeks.
- The vitamin D group had a lower health-related quality of life score compared to the placebo group at 16 and 24 weeks, but this was not significant at eight weeks.

The study is considered low quality due to a high dropout rate in the placebo group. Therefore, it cannot be used to guide clinical practice. More high-quality studies are needed to determine the effects and safety of vitamin D supplementation in people with sickle cell disease.

Six studies were included in a review of asthma patients using daily or intermittent inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). A total of 1211 patients were involved in these high-quality trials, which lasted for 12 to 52 weeks. The analysis showed that there was no significant difference in the risk of experiencing one or more asthma exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids between the two groups (daily vs intermittent ICS). Similarly, there were no differences in serious adverse health events, quality of life, airway hyper-reactivity, hospitalizations, emergency department visits, or withdrawals.

However, compared to daily ICS use, patients using intermittent ICS had a smaller improvement in change from baseline peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR), fewer symptom-free days, more asthma control days, increased use of rescue β2-agonists, and greater increase in exhaled nitric oxide. In paediatric trials, intermittent ICS was associated with greater growth compared to daily treatment.

There is low quality evidence suggesting that both treatments are similarly effective in the use of rescue oral corticosteroids and the rate of severe adverse health events for children and adults with persistent asthma and preschool children suspected of persistent asthma. However, daily ICS was superior to intermittent ICS in several indicators of lung function, airway inflammation, asthma control, and reliever use. Both treatments appeared safe, but a modest growth suppression was associated with daily, compared to intermittent, inhaled budesonide and beclomethasone.

Clinicians should carefully weigh the potential benefits and harm of each treatment option, considering the unknown long-term impact of intermittent therapy on lung growth and lung function decline.

We looked at nine studies with a total of 593 preterm babies who were changing from tube to oral feeding. The studies compared responsive feeding (feeding only when the baby shows signs of hunger) with scheduled interval regimens (feeding at regular intervals). The studies had some issues, such as not being blinded and not assessing all randomized participants. 

Meta-analyses showed that responsive feeding may lead to slower weight gain and could help babies start oral feeding a few days earlier. However, the impact on hospital stay was not strong or consistent. There is low quality evidence that babies fed in response to hunger cues reach full oral feeding faster than those fed set volumes at scheduled intervals. This finding should be interpreted carefully due to study limitations. A large study is needed to confirm this result and see if responsive feeding affects other important outcomes for preterm infants and their families.

Two new studies and five existing ones were included in a review of pregabalin as a treatment for fibromyalgia. Pregabalin increased the number of participants experiencing substantial or moderate pain relief compared to placebo. A small study found no difference between nightly and twice-daily dosing. Two other studies had an enriched enrolment randomised withdrawal design, where those with good pain relief after titration were randomised to continue effective dose or a short down-titration to placebo. Of those randomised, 40% had maintained therapeutic response (MTR) with pregabalin and 20% with placebo. The NNT for MTR was 5, but normalised to the starting population tested it was 12. Specific adverse events were more common with pregabalin than placebo, including dizziness, somnolence, weight gain, and peripheral oedema. Withdrawals due to adverse events were about 10% higher with pregabalin than placebo, but withdrawals due to lack of efficacy were about 6% lower. Pregabalin 300 to 600 mg produces a major reduction in pain intensity over 12 to 26 weeks for a small proportion of people (about 10% more than placebo) with moderate or severe fibromyalgia pain, similar to other effective medicines in fibromyalgia.

We looked at five studies with a total of 240 children aged one to 18 years with mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The studies were done in specialized clinics and follow-up time ranged from six weeks to four months. Three studies compared intranasal steroids to placebo, and two studies compared oral montelukast to placebo. 

We are uncertain about the difference in OSA symptoms between children receiving intranasal corticosteroids compared to placebo (low-certainty evidence). However, children receiving oral montelukast had fewer OSA symptoms compared to those in the placebo group (moderate-certainty evidence). 

Children receiving oral montelukast also had a lower respiratory arousal index and higher oxygen saturation compared to those in the placebo group (moderate and high certainty, respectively). We are uncertain about the difference in desaturation index between children receiving montelukast and placebo (low-certainty evidence). 

Adverse events were rare, minor, and evenly distributed between study groups. No study examined the avoidance of surgical treatment for OSA as an outcome. 

There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of intranasal corticosteroids for the treatment of OSA in children (low certainty). Montelukast has short-term beneficial effects on OSA symptoms in otherwise healthy, non-obese, surgically untreated children (moderate to high certainty). The clinical significance of these findings is unclear. Long-term efficacy and safety data for anti-inflammatory medications for the treatment of OSA in childhood are not available. Patient-centered outcomes such as concentration ability, vigilance, or school performance have not been investigated yet. There are currently no studies on the use of other kinds of anti-inflammatory medications for the treatment of OSA in children. Future RCTs should investigate sustainability of treatment effects, avoidance of surgical treatment for OSA, and long-term safety of anti-inflammatory medications for the treatment of OSA in children, and include patient-centered outcomes.

We looked at 13 studies with 1316 participants who were incontinent for urine, stool, or both and lived in nursing homes or were hospitalized. Most studies had a small sample size and short follow-up periods, and the overall risk of bias was high. The data was not consistent enough for a meta-analysis due to differences in participant population, skin care products, procedures, outcomes, and measurement tools. We found low to moderate quality evidence from two trials that soap and water were not effective in preventing or treating incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD). A skin cleanser or a structured skin care procedure with cleansing, moisturizing, and protecting properties might be more effective than soap and water. Other trials suggest that applying leave-on products like moisturizers or skin protectants may be more effective than not using them. No trial reported on the number of participants not satisfied with treatment or adverse effects. There is little evidence of low to moderate quality on the effects of interventions for preventing and treating IAD in adults. High-quality confirmatory trials are needed to determine the best prevention and treatment regimens for IAD.

We looked at 12 studies with a total of 984 participants who had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The studies compared practicing Tai Chi to doing other activities or no activity. Most studies did not have any issues with the way they were designed or conducted, and none reported any harm from practicing Tai Chi.

The results showed that:

1. Practicing Tai Chi alone improved walking distance and lung function in people with COPD when compared to not doing anything. However, it is unclear if Tai Chi helps reduce shortness of breath or improve quality of life for these individuals. There is also not enough data to determine the impact of Tai Chi on maximal exercise capacity, balance, and muscle strength.
2. Practicing Tai Chi along with other interventions (like breathing exercises or regular exercise) did not show any additional benefits when compared to doing those interventions alone.

Overall, the evidence suggests that practicing Tai Chi can improve functional capacity and lung function in people with COPD when compared to no activity. However, more research is needed to find the most effective style and number of forms of Tai Chi for this group.

A single trial with 75 participants compared doing early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (surgery to remove the gallbladder) within 24 hours of diagnosis, to doing delayed surgery after a waiting period of around 4 months. The trial had a high risk of bias. 

There were no deaths in the early group, while one person died in the delayed group. There were also more complications during the waiting period for the delayed group, including pancreatitis, empyema of the gallbladder, gallbladder perforation, acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, obstructive jaundice, and recurrent biliary colic. 

Overall, there were more serious adverse events in the delayed group (22.5%) compared to the early group (0%). The trial did not report on quality of life or return to work. 

The early group had a shorter hospital stay and operating time compared to the delayed group. Based on this one high-bias risk trial, early laparoscopic cholecystectomy decreases morbidity during the waiting period for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, as well as the hospital stay and operating time. However, more randomized clinical trials are necessary to confirm these findings.

Six studies looked at how zinc affects pneumonia in over 5000 people. The results showed that taking zinc supplements reduced the chance of getting pneumonia by 13% and the prevalence (the number of cases) of pneumonia by 41%. However, these findings are based on low-quality evidence. Further analysis revealed that zinc was effective in reducing pneumonia defined by specific clinical criteria, such as confirmation by chest examination or chest radiograph, but it had no effect on lower specificity pneumonia case definition. In summary, zinc supplementation in children is associated with a reduction in the incidence and prevalence of pneumonia, particularly when pneumonia is confirmed by chest examination or chest radiograph.

Four studies looked at ways to improve adherence to HIV medication in children. No single method was studied twice. Two trials were done in low-income countries. Two trials were randomized, and two were not. A home-based nursing program increased knowledge and medication refills (p=.002), but it did not affect CD4 count or viral load. Caregiver medication diaries did not significantly improve the number of missed doses reported (85% vs. 92%, p=.08) or CD4 percentage or viral load. A peer support group for adolescents did not change self-reported adherence, but the percentage of participants with suppressed viral load increased from 30% to 80% (p=.06). Children on a lopinavir-ritonavir (LPV/r) regimen had better virological suppression than those on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-containing regimens (p=.002), even though adherence was similar. A home-based nursing intervention might improve ART adherence, but more evidence is needed. Medication diaries do not seem to affect adherence or disease outcomes. Two interventions, an LPV/r-containing regimen and peer support therapy for adolescents, did not show improvements in adherence, yet demonstrated greater viral load suppression compared to control groups, suggesting a different mechanism for improved health outcomes. More well-designed evaluations of interventions to improve paediatric adherence to ART are needed.

Fifteen studies were included, testing four ways of giving physostigmine to people with Alzheimer's disease. These methods were intravenous infusion, conventional oral form, controlled-release oral form, and a verum skin patch. There were no usable results from the intravenous infusion trials. The few results from the trials of the conventional oral form showed that physostigmine did not work better than a placebo. Two studies using the controlled-release physostigmine found that it was helpful for a specific group of patients, but many people experienced side effects and withdrew from the study. A fixed dose of physostigmine (mean 33 mg/day) was associated with more withdrawals, adverse events, and gastrointestinal complaints compared to placebo, with no benefit on cognition. The double dose of the verum patch (delivering mean dose 12 mg/day) caused more vomiting, nausea, or abdominal cramps, while the lower dose (delivering mean dose 5.7mg/day) led to more gastrointestinal complaints compared with placebo at 24 weeks. There was no difference between physostigmine and placebo for numbers improved. The evidence supporting the use of physostigmine for Alzheimer's disease treatment is limited, as it showed no convincing benefit and adverse effects remained common, leading to a high rate of withdrawal.

Multiple studies were analyzed to see how well fluoxetine, orlistat, and sibutramine work for weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes. Twenty-two trials with a total of 5049 participants were included in the review. Fluoxetine led to an average weight loss of 5.1 kg after 24 to 26 weeks, orlistat resulted in 2.0 kg of weight loss after 12 to 57 weeks, and sibutramine caused a 5.1 kg reduction in weight after 12 to 52 weeks. Glycated hemoglobin also decreased slightly with fluoxetine and orlistat. Side effects were common for all three medications: gastrointestinal issues for orlistat, tremors, somnolence, and sweating for fluoxetine, and palpitations for sibutramine.

Studies on mazindol, phenmetrazine, and phentermine showed significant weight loss in some cases, but there was not enough data to include them in the analysis. No studies were found on pseudoephedrine, ephedra, sertraline, yohimbine, amphetamine or its derivatives, bupropion, topiramate, benzocaine, threachlorocitric acid, sertraline, and bromocriptine.

Fluoxetine, orlistat, and sibutramine can help people with type 2 diabetes lose weight, but the amount of weight lost is modest and the long-term health benefits are unclear. The safety of sibutramine is uncertain. There is limited information on other drugs for weight loss or control in this population.

In this review, 65 studies (involving 3598 participants) from 2019 or earlier were analyzed. These studies looked at different treatments for bone disease in kidney transplant recipients, including bisphosphonates, vitamin D compounds, teriparatide, denosumab, cinacalcet, parathyroidectomy, and calcitonin. The median follow-up period was 12 months. Most studies evaluated bone density or bone-related biomarkers, with some more recent studies also looking at proteinuria and hyperparathyroidism.

Bisphosphonate therapy is usually started in the perioperative transplantation period (within 3 weeks) and regardless of BMD. However, most studies had high or unclear risks of bias, leading to lower certainty in the results. None of the studies were designed to measure treatment effects on fracture, death, cardiovascular outcomes, or graft loss.

Compared to placebo, bisphosphonate therapy administered over 12 months in transplant recipients may prevent fracture (low certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether any other drug class decreased fracture risk. It is also unclear whether interventions for bone disease in kidney transplantation reduce all-cause or cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke, or graft loss. Bisphosphonate therapy may decrease acute graft rejection (low certainty evidence), but it is uncertain whether any other treatment impacts graft rejection.

Bisphosphonates may reduce bone pain (very low certainty evidence) and increase the risk of hypocalcaemia (low certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether vitamin D compounds have any effect on skeletal, cardiovascular, death, or transplant function outcomes. Evidence for the benefits and harms of all other treatments was of very low certainty. Evidence for children and young adolescents was sparse.

Five studies involving 235 breast cancer survivors met the criteria for this review. These studies looked at computer-assisted cognitive training, compensatory strategy training, meditation, and physical activity interventions. All five studies had a high risk of bias. The results showed that both computer-assisted cognitive training and compensatory strategy training may have beneficial effects on cognitive function, mental well-being, and spiritual quality of life. However, there was no clear evidence of an effect on physical or mental well-being immediately or two months after the interventions. Lower mental well-being immediately post-intervention appeared to be observed in patients who received compensatory strategy training compared to wait-list controls. The evidence for physical activity and meditation interventions on cognitive outcomes is unclear. Overall, the available low-quality evidence suggests that non-pharmacological interventions may help reduce the risk of or ameliorate cognitive impairment following systemic cancer treatment. More high-quality studies are needed to come to firmer conclusions about the benefits of this intervention approach in different patient populations.
